title: Design a URL Shortener

options.name: 301 (Permanent)
options.pros: Browsers cache it, saving a round trip to your server on repeat visits
options.cons: You lose control - once cached, you can't change or expire the mapping, and can't count each redirect for analytics

options.name: 302 (Temporary)
options.pros: Every visit hits your server, so you keep analytics and the ability to change or expire the mapping later
options.cons: No browser caching, so slightly more load on your redirect service

statement: Design a service like bit.ly: given a long URL, generate a short alias that redirects to it. This is one of the most common opening system design questions because it's small enough to finish in 45 minutes but touches ID generation, caching, and read/write-skewed data access — three ideas that show up in almost every other design question.

functional: Given a long URL, return a short URL (e.g. `short.ly/aZ9k2`)
Visiting the short URL redirects (HTTP 302) to the original long URL
Optionally support a custom alias and an expiration date
nonFunctional: 100M new short URLs created per day
~100:1 read:write ratio (redirects vastly outnumber creations)
Redirect latency should feel instant (well under 100ms)
Short URLs must be unique and not guessable in sequence

hints: You need a mapping from a short code to a long URL. What's actually hard is generating the short code itself — how do you avoid two users getting the same code?
A short code is just a number in a different textual representation. What if you had a strictly increasing counter and encoded it in a larger alphabet than base-10?

Base62 (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) encoding of an auto-incrementing ID gives you unique, compact, unguessable-in-practice codes without any coordination between servers — as long as the ID source itself is coordinated (e.g. a dedicated ID-generation service or a database sequence).
diagram:
flowchart TB
  Client([Client]) --> LB[Load Balancer]
  LB --> API1[API Server]
  LB --> API2[API Server]
  API1 --> IDGen[ID Generator\nbase62 counter]
  API1 --> Cache[(Redis Cache\nshort -> long URL)]
  API1 --> DB[(Database\nshort_url, long_url, created_at)]
  Cache -.miss.-> DB
  API2 --> Cache
  API2 --> DB

solution.approach:
**ID generation is the core design decision.** Two viable approaches:

1. **Auto-increment counter + base62 encode.** A single source of truth (a dedicated counter service, or a database `AUTO_INCREMENT` sequence) hands out strictly increasing integers. Encode each integer in base62 (62 characters: a-z, A-Z, 0-9) instead of base10 — this is what turns ID `125` into something like `cb`, giving you a short, URL-safe string. 7 base62 characters give you 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion unique codes, comfortably enough. The tricky part is making the counter itself not a single point of failure/bottleneck at 100M writes/day (~1,150 writes/sec average, with spikes) — solved by handing out counter *ranges* to each API server in batches (server A gets IDs 1,000,000-1,000,999, server B gets the next batch), so servers mint IDs locally without a network round-trip per request.

2. **Hash the long URL** (e.g. MD5, take the first 7 characters) and check for collisions, retrying with a different hash segment or salt if the short code is already taken. Simpler to reason about (no shared counter), but requires a uniqueness check against the database on every write, and collision handling adds complexity as the table grows.

The counter+base62 approach is generally preferred in interviews because it guarantees no collisions by construction, and the range-based ID allocation solves the scaling concern cleanly.

**Data model** is a single table: `short_code (PK), long_url, created_at, expires_at (nullable), custom_alias (bool)`. No joins needed — this is about as simple as a schema gets, which is exactly why the interesting parts of this question are elsewhere.

**Read path (the hot path, 100:1 over writes):** cache-aside with Redis in front of the database, keyed by `short_code`. Since short codes are immutable once created (a given code always maps to the same long URL), there's no cache-invalidation problem to solve — cached entries never go stale, so you can cache aggressively with a long TTL (or no TTL at all, relying on LRU eviction).

**Redirect mechanic:** use HTTP 302 (temporary redirect), not 301 (permanent) — 301 responses get cached by browsers themselves, which means your analytics (click counts, etc.) would stop seeing repeat visits after the first one, and you'd lose the ability to change the mapping or add expiration later.

**Scaling the redirect path further:** since reads dominate 100:1, this is a great candidate for read replicas of the database (in case of a cache miss) and horizontally scaling API servers behind the load balancer — the service is stateless once you've solved ID generation, so scaling out is just adding more API instances.
keyPoints: Counter + base62 encoding gives collision-free, compact short codes; hand out ID ranges per server to avoid a shared-counter bottleneck.
The data model is a single flat table — the complexity here is in ID generation and read scaling, not the schema.
Short-code -> long-URL mappings never change, so caching is simple: no invalidation problem, cache aggressively.
Use HTTP 302 (temporary), not 301, so you keep control over analytics and the ability to change/expire mappings.

practicePrompt: Before reading the solution above: sketch your own high-level design. In particular, think through what happens if two API servers try to create a short URL at the exact same moment — how does your ID-generation approach avoid them colliding?

title: Design a Rate Limiter

options.name: Fixed Window Counter
options.pros: Simplest to implement and reason about
options.cons: Edge-burst problem - up to 2x the limit can slip through right at a window boundary

options.name: Sliding Window
options.pros: Fixes the edge-burst problem the fixed window has
options.cons: More computation and state to track per client

options.name: Token Bucket
options.pros: Allows short bursts cleanly while still enforcing a steady average rate
options.cons: Requires tracking a token count plus a last-refill timestamp per client

statement:
Design a rate limiter that protects an API from being overwhelmed by any single client — whether that's an abusive script, a buggy retry loop, or a legitimate client that's simply making too many requests. Given a client identifier (API key, user ID, or IP) and a request, the limiter must decide, very quickly, whether to allow or reject it.

This question is asked because it's a compact way to probe whether you can reason about algorithmic trade-offs (which counting scheme is both memory-efficient and fair) alongside a very common distributed-systems problem: how do multiple stateless servers share and atomically update a single piece of state without racing each other.

functional: Limit the number of requests a client can make within a given time window (e.g. 100 requests/minute)
Return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header when the limit is exceeded
Support different limits per API endpoint and per client tier (e.g. free vs paid)
Allow limits to be reconfigured without redeploying services
nonFunctional: 10M+ requests/sec across the platform at peak, with the limiter adding negligible (sub-millisecond) latency per request
Rate-limit state must be shared correctly across many stateless API server instances, not tracked per-instance
Memory-efficient — cannot store an unbounded log of every request per client
Prioritize availability over precision — a rate limiter being briefly too lenient is better than it going down and blocking all traffic

hints: The naive approach — store a timestamp for every request per user — doesn't scale. Think about the minimum state you need to keep per client to know whether they're over the limit.

Two families of algorithms solve this differently: ones that track a budget that refills over time (bucket-based), and ones that track counts within rolling time windows. Consider what happens at window boundaries with a naive fixed-window counter.

Token bucket: each client has a bucket of tokens (capacity = burst limit) that refills at a fixed rate; each request consumes a token, and requests are rejected when the bucket is empty. For distributed enforcement, store each client's bucket state in Redis and use an atomic Lua script to check-and-decrement, avoiding race conditions across concurrent requests.
diagram:
flowchart TB
  Client([Client]) --> GW[API Gateway]
  GW --> RL[Rate Limiter\nMiddleware]
  RL --> Redis[(Redis\nclient_id -> tokens, timestamp)]
  RL -->|allowed| Service1[Backend Service]
  RL -->|allowed| Service2[Backend Service]
  RL -.429 rejected.-> Client
  Config[Config Service\nper-tier limits] --> RL

solution.approach:
**The core decision is which rate-limiting algorithm to use, and the subtlety is what happens at time-window boundaries.** The naive approach — a fixed window counter that resets to 0 at the start of every minute — is simple but has an edge-burst problem: a client could send 100 requests in the last second of one window and another 100 in the first second of the next, getting 200 requests through in two seconds even though the limit is 100/minute. Two better algorithms fix this differently. **Token bucket**: each client has a bucket with a fixed capacity (the burst allowance) that refills at a steady rate (e.g. 10 tokens/sec); each request consumes one token and is rejected when the bucket is empty. This naturally allows short bursts up to the bucket size while enforcing a long-run average rate. **Sliding window** (log or counter): a sliding window log keeps a timestamp per request and counts how many fall within the last N seconds (accurate but memory-heavy), while a sliding window counter approximates this by weighting the previous window's count based on how far into the current window you are (cheap and accurate enough for almost all use cases). Token bucket is the most common interview answer because it's cheap to store (just two numbers) and naturally expresses a burst allowance that maps well to real API tiers.

**Where the limiter sits matters as much as the algorithm.** At the API gateway, a single check protects the whole system uniformly and rejects abusive traffic before it ever reaches a backend — cheap and early, but coarse, since the gateway may not know that a search query costs far more than a status check even if both hit the same limit. Per-service rate limiting allows endpoint-specific limits tuned to actual cost, but duplicates the shared-state problem across more places. Most real systems use both: a coarse global/per-client limit at the gateway to stop obvious abuse cheaply, plus finer per-endpoint limits closer to expensive operations.

**Distributed enforcement is the hard systems part.** With many API server instances behind a load balancer, a client's requests land on different servers across their session, so in-memory per-server counters can't see the client's true global rate — a client could get 100 requests through each of 10 servers before any one of them thinks it's over the limit. The fix is centralizing rate-limit state in a fast shared store; Redis is the standard choice, since its single-threaded execution and support for atomic operations avoid a whole class of race conditions. A naive `GET count; if count < limit: INCR count` is not atomic across the two calls and lets two concurrent requests both read 'under limit' and both proceed, overshooting. The fix is a small Lua script executed via `EVAL`, which Redis guarantees runs as one atomic unit with no other command interleaving.

**The per-client state is deliberately tiny.** For token bucket: `{tokens_remaining, last_refill_timestamp}` per key (e.g. `ratelimit:{user_id}:{endpoint}`). On each request, the Lua script computes how many tokens should have accrued since the last refill given the refill rate, adds them (capped at bucket capacity), then checks and decrements if a token is available. This is O(1) per request regardless of elapsed time, and needs no background reset job — the state self-corrects on next access. A TTL roughly equal to the refill period lets inactive clients' state expire naturally rather than accumulating forever.

**What happens when Redis is unavailable is a real design decision, not an afterthought.** Since the requirements explicitly prioritize availability over precision, the system should generally **fail open** — if the backing store can't be reached within a tight timeout, let the request through rather than rejecting all traffic because of a dependency outage. A rate limiter's job is to protect the system from abuse, but one that becomes a single point of failure and takes down all traffic is a worse outcome than briefly under-enforcing limits. Especially sensitive endpoints (a login endpoint under brute-force attempt) might instead fail closed, accepting the availability hit as the lesser evil — this should be configurable per endpoint, not a single global choice.

**At very high volumes, even Redis can become a bottleneck** if every request needs a network round trip. A common optimization is two-level: each API server keeps a small local, approximate counter and only consults Redis periodically or when near the limit, trading a little precision for much less network chatter. Redis itself can also be sharded by client ID using the same consistent-hashing technique used for distributed caches, so no single instance holds the whole platform's state. Limits themselves should live in a small, cacheable config store, read-through cached by the limiter, so operators can change a tier or threshold without a deploy.
keyPoints: Token bucket handles burst allowance cleanly; fixed-window counters have an edge-burst problem that sliding window approaches fix
Rate-limit state must be centralized (e.g. Redis) since a client's requests land on different, stateless API servers
Check-and-increment must be atomic (a Lua script) — separate GET+INCR calls create a race condition that lets clients exceed the limit
Gateway-level limiting protects the whole system cheaply and early; per-service limiting allows finer, cost-aware control — most real systems use both
Prefer failing open over failing closed when the rate limiter's backing store is unreachable, since availability was prioritized
Per-client state is tiny (two or three fields) and self-expiring via TTL, not a growing log of every request
At extreme scale, a local-approximate-plus-periodic-sync layer in front of Redis cuts network round trips at the cost of slight precision

practicePrompt: Should Redis being reachable be a hard requirement for the rate limiter, or should the API gateway fail open and let requests through when it isn't? Think through the answer for a public read-only content API versus a login endpoint under brute-force attempt, then decide whether that should be a single global policy or configurable per endpoint.

title: Design a Chat Application (WhatsApp)

tradeoffs.question: How does the client receive new messages?

options.name: Long-Polling
options.pros: Works everywhere, including behind old proxies/firewalls that block persistent connections
options.cons: Higher latency and more request overhead - the client keeps re-requesting

options.name: WebSockets
options.pros: True server push over a single persistent connection - low latency, low overhead
options.cons: Needs a connection registry (which server holds which user's socket) and doesn't work in every restrictive network

tradeoffs.chosen: WebSockets, with long-polling as the fallback

statement:
Design the backend for a real-time messaging app like WhatsApp: users can message each other one-on-one or in groups, messages should arrive within a fraction of a second when both parties are online, and no message should ever be silently lost — including when the recipient is offline and comes back hours later.

This question is asked because it forces you to move past request/response HTTP thinking into server-initiated, stateful communication, and it touches message ordering, delivery guarantees, and the operational reality of holding millions of persistent connections open at once — concepts that generalize to almost any real-time system.

functional: Send and receive text messages in real time between two users
Support group chats with multiple participants
Show message delivery status: sent, delivered, and read receipts
Deliver queued messages to a user when they come back online
Show basic online/offline presence status
nonFunctional: 500M daily active users sending ~40 messages/day each — billions of messages/day
Message delivery latency under 200ms for online recipients
Messages must never be lost, even if a client disconnects mid-send
Strong ordering of messages within a single conversation
High availability — chat is core functionality and must survive individual server failures

hints: A request/response HTTP model doesn't let the server push a message to a recipient who didn't ask for it. What kind of connection lets the server initiate data transfer to the client?

You need to track which server holds the open connection for each user, since a user's live connection lands on one specific server out of many. How do you route a message from the sender's server to the recipient's server?

Maintain a connection registry (e.g. in Redis) mapping user_id -> server_id for whichever server holds a user's live connection. When server A needs to deliver to a user connected on server B, it publishes to a message broker/pub-sub channel that server B is subscribed to. For offline users, write to a persistent per-user inbox/queue that's drained on reconnect.
diagram:
flowchart TB
  ClientA([Sender]) -->|WebSocket| GWA[Chat Server A]
  ClientB([Recipient]) -->|WebSocket| GWB[Chat Server B]
  GWA --> Registry[(Connection Registry\nuser_id -> server_id)]
  GWA --> Broker[Message Broker\nPub/Sub]
  Broker --> GWB
  GWA --> MsgDB[(Message Store\nconversation_id, sender, ts)]
  GWB --> Inbox[(Offline Inbox Queue)]
  Inbox -.on reconnect.-> GWB

solution.approach:
**The core decision is the transport: you need the server to push data to a client that didn't ask for anything, which plain request/response HTTP can't do.** A WebSocket is a persistent, full-duplex TCP connection between client and server — once established, either side can send a message at any time with no new handshake, which is exactly what 'push a message the instant it arrives' requires. For clients or networks that can't hold a WebSocket open, long-polling is the fallback: the client makes a request the server holds open until there's a message to deliver (or a timeout), then immediately reopens it. A production design typically defaults to WebSocket and falls back to long-polling.

**Because each user's live connection is held open on exactly one specific server, routing a message from sender to recipient becomes a real distributed-systems problem.** If Alice is connected to chat server A and sends a message to Bob, who's connected to chat server B, server A has no direct way to reach Bob's socket — it doesn't even know which server Bob is on. The fix is a connection registry: a shared, fast lookup (Redis is a natural fit) mapping `user_id -> server_id`, updated whenever a user connects or disconnects. Server A looks up Bob, finds he's on server B, and needs a way to actually get the message there.

**A message broker (pub/sub) is what actually moves the message between servers.** Rather than server A opening a direct connection to every other chat server, each chat server subscribes to a channel tied to its own server ID on a broker like Redis Pub/Sub or Kafka. Server A publishes 'deliver this to Bob' to the broker; server B, subscribed to the right channel, receives it and pushes it down Bob's open connection. This decouples the chat servers from each other entirely — none of them need to know how many other servers exist or where any other user is connected beyond the registry lookup.

**Delivery and read receipts are a layer on top of the base delivery mechanism, not the mechanism itself.** A message moves through distinct states: `sent` (the client's local optimistic state, before the server even acknowledges it), `delivered` (the server has handed it to the recipient's device, or queued it if offline), and `read` (the recipient's client has actually displayed it, itself a small event sent back through the same pipeline in reverse). Each of these should be idempotent and tolerate being received twice, since retries happen at every layer.

**Ordering and deduplication rely on identifiers assigned at two different points.** The client generates a unique message ID (a UUID) when the user hits send, before any network round trip — this is what lets a retried send be recognized as the same message rather than creating a duplicate. Separately, the server assigns a monotonically increasing sequence number per conversation when it persists the message — this, not wall-clock timestamps (which can be skewed across servers/devices), is what guarantees consistent ordering within a conversation.

**Offline delivery is what makes the message store more than a cache.** Every message is durably written to a message store keyed by conversation, regardless of whether the recipient is currently connected. For an offline recipient, the message also lands in a lightweight per-user inbox/queue; when that user reconnects, their server queries the backlog (messages newer than their last-synced sequence number per conversation) and delivers it before resuming live delivery — so 'online' and 'offline' delivery are really the same write path with two different read/notify paths layered on top.

**Group chat is 1:1 delivery fanned out to N participants.** A message to a group is written once, then delivery is attempted to each participant's connection (or queued for each offline participant) individually. For very large groups this write fan-out gets expensive, and the interesting extension is applying the same push-vs-pull trade-off discussed in the news-feed design.

**Scaling connection count is mostly horizontal scaling with sticky sessions plus low per-connection overhead.** A single well-tuned server can hold hundreds of thousands to low millions of idle connections; the fleet scales by adding more servers behind a connection-aware load balancer. Heartbeats let a server detect a dead connection quickly and update the registry, rather than waiting on a TCP timeout that could take minutes and leave the registry pointing at a socket that's already gone.
keyPoints: WebSockets provide real server-push delivery; long-polling is the fallback for clients that can't hold one open
A connection registry maps user -> server, since each user's live connection lives on exactly one server at a time
A pub/sub broker routes messages between chat servers without them needing to know about each other directly
Client-generated message IDs give idempotency; server-assigned per-conversation sequence numbers give ordering
A persistent per-user inbox guarantees delivery to offline users — online and offline delivery share the same write path
Delivery and read receipts are acks layered on top of the base delivery mechanism, not separate systems
Group chat fan-out at write time trades write cost for fast reads, same trade-off as a news feed

practicePrompt: Think through what happens if a user is connected to server A, sends a message, but the message broker briefly can't reach server B (the recipient's server). How would you guarantee at-least-once delivery without duplicating messages the recipient already got?

title: Design a Twitter-like News Feed

tradeoffs.question: How is the feed assembled - at post time or at read time?

options.name: Fan-out on Write
options.pros: Reads are fast - a user's feed is already precomputed and waiting
options.cons: A celebrity with millions of followers turns one post into millions of writes

options.name: Fan-out on Read
options.pros: Writes are cheap regardless of follower count
options.cons: Reads are expensive - merging posts from everyone a user follows, on every feed load

options.name: Hybrid
options.pros: Push for normal users (fast reads), pull-and-merge only for celebrity accounts - avoids both failure modes
options.cons: More implementation complexity - two code paths instead of one

statement:
Design the backend that powers a user's home timeline on a platform like Twitter: users follow other users, post short updates, and expect their feed to show recent posts from the people they follow without a noticeable delay when they open the app.

This question is asked because the obvious, naive solution — query posts from everyone a user follows, every time they open the feed — falls apart at scale in a very specific and instructive way: a small number of extremely popular accounts break the assumptions that make the simple version work, and reasoning through that failure and its fix is the entire point of the exercise.

functional: Users can post short text updates
Users can follow other users
A user's home feed shows recent posts from people they follow, roughly reverse-chronological or ranked
The feed updates with new posts without feeling laggy when reopened
nonFunctional: 200M daily active users, averaging 200 follows each, with some celebrity accounts having 50M+ followers
Feed load latency under 200ms at p99
Reads vastly outnumber writes — users check feeds far more often than they post
Eventual consistency is acceptable — a new post appearing a few seconds late in a follower's feed is fine
Must handle a heavily skewed, power-law follower distribution without degrading for everyone else

hints: Two ways to build a feed: compute it when the user posts (push it into every follower's feed), or compute it when a follower opens their feed (pull from everyone they follow and merge). Think about the read:write ratio here.
Fan-out on write is fast to read, but what happens when someone with 50 million followers posts? Fan-out on read avoids that but makes every feed load expensive — can you combine them?
Hybrid: fan-out on write for regular users, precomputing followers' feeds. Exempt accounts above a follower threshold — pull their posts at read time and merge with the precomputed feed.
diagram:
flowchart TB
  User([User]) -->|post| PostSvc[Post Service]
  PostSvc --> PostDB[(Posts Store)]
  PostSvc --> FanoutQ[Fan-out Queue]
  FanoutQ --> FanoutW[Fan-out Worker]
  FanoutW --> FeedCache[(Feed Cache\nuser_id -> post_ids)]
  FanoutW -.skip celebrities.-> FeedCache
  Reader([User]) -->|open feed| FeedSvc[Feed Service]
  FeedSvc --> FeedCache
  FeedSvc -->|merge celebrity posts| PostDB
  FeedSvc --> Ranker[Ranking Service]

solution.approach:
**The core decision is when feed content gets computed: at post time (fan-out on write) or at read time (fan-out on read/pull).** Fan-out on write means that the instant a user posts, the system immediately pushes that post's ID into the precomputed feed of every one of their followers — reading a feed later is then just fetching a precomputed list, extremely fast. Fan-out on read means posts are written once, and a feed is assembled on demand by pulling recent posts from everyone the viewer follows and merging them — writing is trivially cheap, but every feed load does work proportional to how many people you follow.

**The trade-off looks fine until you account for a wildly skewed follower distribution.** Given the read-dominated ratio, fan-out on write is attractive — do the expensive work once at write time since it'll be read many times. But apply that literally to an account with 50 million followers, and a single post triggers 50 million writes, all fired from one request, creating a massive, bursty write-amplification problem plus 50 million redundant copies of the same post ID sitting in caches. This is the celebrity problem, and it's the crux of the question.

**The fix is a hybrid, threshold-based approach.** For accounts under some follower-count threshold — the overwhelming majority of users — stick with fan-out on write, precomputing and pushing into followers' feed caches asynchronously. For accounts above the threshold, skip fan-out entirely; instead, at read time, merge their recent posts directly into the viewer's feed by pulling from the small list of celebrities the viewer follows. Since a typical user follows at most a handful of true celebrities, this read-time merge touches only a few extra sources, not the whole follow graph — you get fan-out on write's fast reads for the common case and avoid its worst-case write blowup for the rare, extreme case.

**The data model separates the source of truth (posts) from the read-optimized structure (the feed cache).** A `Posts` store holds actual content once, keyed by post ID. A `FeedCache` (typically Redis, one sorted set per user scored by timestamp) holds only post IDs — not full content — for a bounded recent window (say, the most recent 500-1000 post IDs). A separate `Follows` graph drives fan-out and the pull-side merge. Keeping the feed cache to IDs only keeps it small enough to live comfortably in memory even at hundreds of millions of users.

**Fan-out itself runs asynchronously, off the posting request's critical path.** When a regular user posts, the post is written to the `Posts` store and the write returns success immediately; a background worker pulled from a queue then walks the poster's follower list and pushes the post ID into each follower's feed cache. This means posting stays fast regardless of follower count, and it's also why the system is fine with eventual consistency — a follower might not see a brand-new post for a few seconds while fan-out catches up.

**Reading a feed merges two sources and then ranks.** The feed service fetches the viewer's precomputed feed cache, separately fetches recent posts from any celebrities they follow, merges the two by timestamp, and hands the merged, deduplicated list to a ranking step. A lightweight ranking function scores candidate posts on a mix of recency, predicted engagement, and affinity (how much the viewer historically engages with this author) — this can start as a simple weighted sum and evolve into a learned model later, but the retrieval step above is the harder, more interesting systems problem and is what this question is really testing.

**A capped feed cache creates a real trade-off for users who scroll back far.** Since only the most recent N post IDs are kept per user in the fast cache, scrolling past that point requires falling back to a slower, on-demand pull-based query against the follow graph and post store directly — acceptable, since deep-scrollback is rare, but worth calling out as a deliberate boundary rather than an oversight.
keyPoints: Fan-out on write: fast reads, expensive/unbounded writes for high-follower accounts
Fan-out on read: cheap writes, expensive reads that merge across everyone followed
A hybrid approach handles the celebrity/power-law problem: push for normal users, pull-and-merge for celebrities
The feed cache holds only post IDs, not full content, capped to a bounded recent window
Fan-out runs asynchronously off the write path so posting stays fast regardless of follower count
Eventual consistency is fine — a post can take a few seconds to reach every follower's feed
Ranking is a separate concern layered on top of retrieval — recency, engagement, and affinity signals

practicePrompt: Where would you set the celebrity threshold — the follower count above which you switch to pull-based fan-out — and what breaks if you set it too low or too high? Sketch the read-time merge logic for a feed that combines precomputed posts with 2-3 celebrities' live posts.

title: Design a Notification System
statement:
Design a notification system that lets other services within a company — an order service, a security service, a social service — send a message to a user through whichever channel makes sense (push, SMS, or email) without each of those services having to know anything about how push notifications, SMS, or email actually work.

This question is asked because it's a clean example of designing an internal platform: decoupling event producers from delivery mechanics via queues, isolating failures between independent external dependencies, and guaranteeing at-least-once delivery without it becoming at-least-twice-once from the user's perspective.

functional: Send notifications to users via push notification, SMS, and email
Any internal service can trigger a notification via a simple API/event
Users can configure channel preferences and opt out of notification categories
Avoid sending duplicate notifications for the same underlying event
Track delivery status per notification and per channel
nonFunctional: 100M notifications/day across all channels, with bursts (e.g. a breaking-news push to millions within minutes)
Near-real-time delivery for push (seconds); best-effort for email
Must tolerate a third-party provider outage or rate limit without losing notifications for other channels
At-least-once delivery, with dedup so it never feels like a double-send to the user

hints: Different services trigger notifications for different reasons. What decouples 'something happened' from 'actually send the message'?
A single event might fan out to three channels, each with a different third-party API, rate limit, and failure mode. How do you isolate one channel's slowness or outage from the others?

Producers publish an event to a queue. A dispatcher reads it, checks preferences and dedup, then fans out into per-channel queues (push, SMS, email), each consumed by its own worker pool that talks to the relevant provider (APNs/FCM, Twilio, SES) with retries and exponential backoff, decoupling channels from each other.
diagram:
flowchart TB
  Producer[Internal Service] -->|event| Queue[Notification Queue]
  Queue --> Dispatcher[Dispatcher\nchecks preferences and dedup]
  Dispatcher --> PushQ[Push Queue]
  Dispatcher --> SmsQ[SMS Queue]
  Dispatcher --> EmailQ[Email Queue]
  PushQ --> PushW[Push Worker] --> FCM[FCM / APNs]
  SmsQ --> SmsW[SMS Worker] --> Twilio[Twilio]
  EmailQ --> EmailW[Email Worker] --> SES[SES]
  Dispatcher --> PrefDB[(User Preferences)]
  Dispatcher --> DedupCache[(Dedup Cache\nevent_id)]

solution.approach:
**The core decision is decoupling 'something happened' from 'send a message about it,' via an event queue.** Any internal service that wants to notify a user doesn't call push/SMS/email providers directly — it publishes a lightweight event (`user_id`, `event_type`, relevant data) onto a queue and moves on. The order service, the security service, and every other producer stay completely ignorant of delivery mechanics, provider APIs, user channel preferences, or retry logic; all of that complexity lives in one place downstream.

**A dispatcher consumes those events and is where cross-cutting concerns live.** It looks up the user's notification preferences (which channels are enabled, category-level opt-outs), applies deduplication, decides which channel(s) this event should go out on, and then fans out — not by calling providers itself, but by publishing a per-channel message onto a separate queue per channel (push, SMS, email).

**Separate queues and worker pools per channel are what isolate one provider's problems from the others.** SMS goes through Twilio, push goes through FCM/APNs, email goes through SES — three independent external dependencies with their own rate limits, latencies, and failure modes. If Twilio is having an outage or throttling the account, only the SMS queue backs up; push and email keep flowing normally because they're consumed by entirely separate worker pools with no shared resource between them. Without this separation, a slow or broken channel would create backpressure that stalls notifications on every channel.

**Deduplication uses an idempotency key and a short-lived cache, not the queue's own guarantees.** Most queue systems only promise at-least-once delivery — a producer's own retry after a timeout, or the queue redelivering an unacknowledged message, can both cause the same logical event to be processed twice. Each event carries a unique `event_id`; before dispatching, the dispatcher checks a dedup cache (Redis, with a TTL covering realistic retry windows) for that ID — if it's already there, the event is dropped as a duplicate; if not, it's recorded and processing proceeds.

**Each channel worker handles retries and failure independently, with a dead-letter queue as the backstop.** A transient failure triggers a retry with exponential backoff, capped at some max attempt count; after that, the message moves to a dead-letter queue for investigation and alerting rather than being retried forever or silently dropped. Respecting each provider's own rate limits — a token bucket per provider account, the same mechanism as the rate-limiter question elsewhere in this set — keeps the platform from getting throttled or banned by its own vendors.

**Bursts are absorbed by the queue rather than requiring instant fan-out capacity.** A breaking-news push to millions of users doesn't need to complete in one second — it needs to start promptly and drain at a sustainable rate. Because the dispatcher writes to durable queues rather than calling providers synchronously, a huge spike in events just means deeper queues temporarily; worker pools scale horizontally to drain the backlog faster, but nothing is lost even if draining takes a few minutes under an extreme spike.

**Delivery status is updated asynchronously, after the fact, via provider callbacks — not assumed at send time.** Handing a message to Twilio or SES doesn't mean it was delivered to the end device; these providers typically expose delivery-receipt webhooks that the notification system listens for and uses to update the notification's status after the fact, closing the loop for observability without blocking the send path on it.
keyPoints: Producers publish events; a dispatcher decouples 'what happened' from 'how it's delivered'
A separate queue and worker pool per channel isolates one provider's outage from the others
Idempotency keys plus a dedup cache prevent duplicate sends under at-least-once delivery
User preferences are checked once, centrally, at dispatch time
Failed sends retry with exponential backoff and land in a dead-letter queue after max attempts
Queues absorb burst traffic so workers can drain it at a sustainable throughput
Delivery status updates asynchronously via provider webhooks, not assumed at send time

practicePrompt: A user has both push and email enabled. An order-shipped event fires twice due to an upstream retry. Walk through exactly where in your pipeline the duplicate gets caught before it reaches the dispatch-to-provider step, and what key you'd use to detect it.

title: Design a Distributed Cache

tradeoffs.question: Which eviction policy under memory pressure?

options.name: LRU (Least Recently Used)
options.pros: Cheap to implement (a linked list + hash map) and matches most real access patterns well
options.cons: A single burst of one-time scans can evict genuinely hot keys

options.name: LFU (Least Frequently Used)
options.pros: Resistant to that scan-burst problem - true frequency matters more than recency
options.cons: More bookkeeping per key, and slow to adapt when access patterns shift

statement:
Design a distributed in-memory cache — a simplified version of a Redis or Memcached cluster — that stores key-value pairs across many machines, so no single machine needs to hold the entire dataset in memory, and the cache keeps serving traffic even if an individual node fails.

This question is asked because it isolates a handful of distributed-systems fundamentals — data partitioning, replication, and eviction under resource pressure — from the comparatively easier question of what's actually being cached, letting the interviewer see how you reason about them directly.

functional: GET/SET/DELETE key-value operations with low latency
Data is distributed (sharded) across multiple cache nodes
Support adding or removing nodes without a full cache wipe/rehash
Automatically evict data when a node runs low on memory
nonFunctional: Sub-millisecond read/write latency, 1M+ operations/sec across the cluster
Tolerate individual node failure without losing all data for the keys it held
Roughly even key distribution across nodes, avoiding hot spots
Memory is finite per node — a sane eviction policy is required under pressure

hints: With N nodes, the naive approach hash(key) mod N tells you which node owns a key. What happens to almost every key's assignment when you add or remove one node?
You want adding or removing a node to remap only a small fraction of keys, not nearly all of them. What hashing scheme maps both keys and nodes onto the same conceptual ring?

Consistent hashing: hash both nodes and keys onto a ring; a key belongs to the first node clockwise from its hash position. Adding or removing a node only reassigns the keys between it and its neighbor. Use virtual nodes (multiple ring positions per physical node) to smooth out uneven load distribution.
diagram:
flowchart TB
  Client([Client]) --> Router[Client Library\nconsistent hash ring]
  Router --> NodeA[Cache Node A]
  Router --> NodeB[Cache Node B]
  Router --> NodeC[Cache Node C]
  NodeA -->|replicate| ReplicaA[Replica A]
  NodeB -->|replicate| ReplicaB[Replica B]
  NodeC -->|replicate| ReplicaC[Replica C]
  NodeA --> EvictA[LRU Eviction\nunder memory pressure]

solution.approach:
**The core decision is how keys get distributed across nodes, and the standard naive approach breaks badly when the cluster resizes.** `hash(key) mod N` (N = number of nodes) is simple and gives an even distribution for a fixed N, but the moment N changes — a node is added or removed, which happens routinely for scaling or after a failure — almost every key's `hash(key) mod N` result changes too, meaning nearly the entire cache effectively gets invalidated at once. Every client suddenly asks a different node for data that node has never seen, producing a massive cache-miss stampede against the backing database at exactly the moment the cluster is already in flux.

**Consistent hashing solves this by decoupling 'which node' from a value that shifts wildly when N changes.** Both nodes and keys are hashed onto the same conceptual ring (a fixed, large hash space). A key belongs to whichever node's position comes next going clockwise from the key's own hash position. When a node is added, it only takes over the slice of the ring between itself and its counter-clockwise neighbor — a small, bounded set of keys gets remapped, not the whole keyspace. Removing a node has the mirror effect: its keys fall to the next node clockwise, and again only that slice moves.

**Virtual nodes fix an uneven-distribution problem that plain consistent hashing still has at small N.** With only a handful of physical nodes at a few random ring positions, the arcs between them can be quite uneven by chance, giving some nodes a disproportionate share of keys and load. The standard fix is giving each physical node many positions on the ring (say, 100-200 virtual nodes each) — this averages out to a much more even distribution regardless of physical node count, and means that when a node is removed, its load spreads across many other nodes rather than dumping entirely onto one neighbor.

**Routing can live on the client or behind a proxy, and real systems mostly pick client-side for latency.** A client library holds a view of the ring and computes which node owns a key locally, then talks to that node directly — one network hop. A stateless proxy layer all clients go through instead adds a hop but centralizes ring-membership logic in one place. Either way, something needs to keep the ring view consistent across all participants as nodes join and leave — a coordination service (like ZooKeeper/etcd) or a gossip protocol where nodes exchange membership info peer-to-peer.

**Replication is what actually provides fault tolerance — sharding alone just distributes data, it doesn't protect it.** Each key's data is written not just to its primary node but to N-1 additional replica nodes, typically the next few nodes clockwise on the ring. If the primary for a shard fails, a replica is promoted and traffic continues being served, just from a different node, while the failed node is replaced and catches back up. Replication is usually asynchronous for a cache — strict synchronous replication would add latency to every write, defeating the point of a low-latency cache — which means a very recent write could be lost if the primary fails before replicating, an acceptable trade-off since the cache isn't the system of record.

**Eviction handles the case where a node's memory fills up regardless of how well data is distributed.** Each node applies its own local policy — LRU is the most common, often implemented approximately via sampling rather than maintaining a perfectly ordered structure, since exact LRU tracking has real overhead at high throughput. LFU is an alternative when access frequency matters more than recency for the workload.

**A single very popular key is a problem consistent hashing doesn't solve, because it's not a distribution problem.** Even with perfectly even key distribution, if one specific key gets a disproportionate share of all traffic — a trending item, a viral post — the one node or replica set owning it can still be overwhelmed while every other node sits idle. This needs a different technique layered on top: replicating that hot key to many/all nodes, or letting clients cache it locally for a very short TTL to absorb read pressure before it ever reaches the distributed cache.

**It's worth being explicit that the cache is not the source of truth.** It sits in front of a database following the cache-aside pattern — check cache, on miss read the database and populate the cache — which is why losing a bit of cached data on node failure, or serving a slightly stale value, is tolerable in a way that losing rows from the actual database would not be.
keyPoints: Consistent hashing bounds the fraction of keys remapped when nodes are added or removed, unlike hash mod N
Virtual nodes spread load evenly even with a small number of physical nodes
Replication (leader plus followers per shard) keeps data available across a node failure
Memory is finite — LRU/LFU eviction reclaims space under pressure, trading capacity for potential cache misses
A single very popular key can still create a hot spot even with perfectly even hashing; solved separately (e.g. client-side caching of hot keys)
The cache is not the source of truth — correctness of the underlying data lives in the database

practicePrompt: Sketch how your client library discovers that a node has been added to the ring and starts routing some keys to it — and what happens to a GET for a key that hashed to the old node but now maps to the new one, which doesn't have the data yet?

title: Design an E-commerce Checkout and Order System

tradeoffs.question: How do the saga's steps coordinate?

options.name: Choreography
options.pros: No single coordinator - services react to each other's events directly, less central infrastructure
options.cons: The overall flow is implicit and scattered across services - hard to see or reason about the whole saga in one place

options.name: Orchestration
options.pros: One place owns the flow and its state machine - easy to reason about, resume, and debug
options.cons: The orchestrator is a new central component, and every service must integrate with it

statement:
Design the backend for an e-commerce checkout flow: a customer has items in their cart, clicks 'place order,' and the system needs to confirm the items are actually in stock, charge their payment method, and create a confirmed order — with none of those three things happening in isolation from the others going wrong.

This question is asked because it's the canonical example of a business transaction that spans multiple independently-owned services and databases, where you can't reach for a single database transaction to make the whole thing atomic, and getting the failure-handling wrong has directly visible consequences: overselling a product, or charging a customer's card twice.

functional: User adds items to a cart and proceeds to checkout
System reserves inventory for the items so two customers can't buy the last unit
Process payment for the order
Create a confirmed order and trigger fulfillment/shipping
Roll back cleanly (release inventory, refund) if any step fails
nonFunctional: Never oversell inventory — this is the hard constraint
Never double-charge a customer, even under network retries
Checkout should complete in a few seconds end-to-end under normal load
Handle flash-sale-style spikes — thousands of concurrent checkouts for the same limited-stock item
Order, inventory, and payment naturally live in separate services and databases — no single ACID transaction spans all of them

hints: Inventory count, payment processing, and order creation almost certainly live in different services with different databases. What technique coordinates a multi-step transaction when you can't use a single database transaction across all of them?

For the 'never oversell' constraint specifically: think about what has to happen atomically at the moment of checkout, before payment even runs, to guarantee the item is actually available to this specific customer.

Reserve inventory first — atomically, before charging payment. Use the saga pattern: a sequence of local transactions (reserve inventory -> charge payment -> create order), each with a compensating action (release inventory, refund payment) that runs if a later step fails. Idempotency keys on the payment charge request prevent a network retry from double-charging.
diagram:
flowchart TB
  Client([Customer]) --> Checkout[Checkout Service\nsaga orchestrator]
  Checkout --> Inventory[Inventory Service]
  Inventory --> InvDB[(Inventory DB\nreservations)]
  Checkout --> Payment[Payment Service]
  Payment --> PSP[Payment Provider]
  Checkout --> OrderSvc[Order Service]
  OrderSvc --> OrderDB[(Orders DB)]
  Checkout -.compensate.-> Inventory
  Checkout -.compensate.-> Payment
  OrderSvc --> Fulfillment[Fulfillment Queue]

solution.approach:
**The core decision is how to coordinate a single logical transaction that spans multiple independently-owned services and databases, since a normal ACID transaction can't span them.** Inventory, payment, and orders are naturally separate services — different teams, different databases — and there's no way to wrap 'reserve inventory,' 'charge card,' and 'create order' in one atomic commit the way you could if they were tables in the same database. The saga pattern is the standard answer: break the transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each owned by one service, where every step has a corresponding compensating action that undoes it if a later step fails.

**Orchestration vs. choreography is a real implementation choice within sagas.** In an orchestration-based saga, a single coordinator (the checkout service) explicitly calls each step in order and explicitly triggers compensations on failure — straightforward to reason about and debug, since the whole flow's logic lives in one place. In a choreography-based saga, each service instead reacts to events published by the previous step, avoiding a central coordinator but making the overall flow harder to trace, since it's implicit in a web of event subscriptions. For a flow this linear and business-critical, orchestration is usually the better fit.

**Inventory reservation is the specific mechanic that satisfies the 'never oversell' hard constraint, and it has to happen atomically before payment.** The simplest version is a conditional atomic update — `UPDATE inventory SET available = available - 1 WHERE product_id = ? AND available > 0` — then checking whether any row was actually affected; if zero rows changed, the item was out of stock and checkout fails immediately, before payment is ever attempted. A richer version inserts an explicit reservation row with a short TTL (e.g. 10 minutes) rather than directly decrementing a count, which naturally handles cart abandonment: if the customer never completes checkout, the reservation simply expires and the stock becomes available again without any explicit cleanup step.

**Under flash-sale-style contention, that single inventory row becomes a hot spot, and the interesting scaling question is what to do about it.** Thousands of concurrent checkout attempts racing to update the same product row create heavy lock contention even though the update itself is cheap. Options include sharding the available-count across several counters that sum to the true total, or — more robustly for a truly hot item — funneling checkout attempts for that specific product through a single ordered queue/worker so requests are serialized deliberately rather than racing a database row directly, converting lock contention into queue wait time, which is easier to reason about and degrade gracefully under.

**Payment idempotency is what prevents a network retry from becoming a double charge.** The checkout orchestrator generates a unique idempotency key per checkout attempt and passes it to the payment provider's charge API. Payment providers that support idempotency keys (Stripe, for example) guarantee that multiple charge requests with the same key result in exactly one actual charge, returning the original result on any retry — this is what makes it safe for the orchestrator to retry a payment call after a timeout without knowing whether the first attempt actually succeeded on the provider's end.

**The data model tracks state explicitly enough to resume a saga after a crash.** `Orders` (order_id, user_id, status, total, idempotency_key), `OrderItems`, `InventoryReservations` (reservation_id, product_id, quantity, expires_at, status), and `Payments` (payment_id, order_id, provider_charge_id, status) each carry enough state that the order's overall status — `pending` -> `inventory_reserved` -> `payment_charged` -> `confirmed`, or a failure branch at any step — is durable and re-derivable. This matters because the orchestrator itself can crash mid-saga; on restart, it needs to look at an order's persisted state and know exactly which step to resume or compensate from.

**Failure handling means picking the right compensation for each step, and they're not symmetric.** If payment fails after inventory was reserved, the compensation is straightforward: release the reservation. If order creation fails after payment already succeeded, the safer compensating action is usually to retry order creation — since creating the order record is naturally idempotent — rather than immediately refunding, since a refund followed by a successful late retry would leave the customer paying nothing for a fulfilled order. Issuing a refund should be the fallback only after retries of the downstream step are exhausted.

**The consistency model is deliberately layered: eventually consistent overall, strongly consistent at the one step that actually matters.** The order as a whole is in a transient 'processing' state for the second or two the saga takes to run — that's fine. But the inventory reservation step specifically must be atomic and strongly consistent, because that's the actual mechanism preventing two customers from being sold the same last unit; every other step can be eventually reconciled after the fact, but an oversold item can't be un-sold without a customer-facing problem.
keyPoints: No single ACID transaction spans inventory, payment, and order services — the saga pattern chains local transactions with compensating actions
Inventory must be atomically reserved at checkout start, before payment runs, to guarantee no overselling
Idempotency keys on the payment charge prevent double-charging under client/network retries
Orchestration-based sagas are easier to reason about for a critical, mostly-linear flow than choreography
Reservations carry a TTL so abandoned checkouts automatically release inventory back to the pool
Persist the saga's state machine so a crashed orchestrator can resume rather than leaving an order stuck
Flash-sale contention on one hot product may need serialization (a queue) rather than relying purely on optimistic DB updates

practicePrompt: Walk through the failure case where payment succeeds but the order-creation step then fails (e.g. the order service is briefly down). Should the compensating action be a refund, or a retry of order creation? What determines which is safer here?

title: Design a Ride-Sharing App (Uber)
statement:
Design the backend for a ride-sharing app like Uber: riders request a trip from their current location, the system finds and matches them with a nearby available driver, and both parties can see each other's live location and an ETA throughout the trip.

This question is asked because most engineers haven't had to reason about geospatial data at scale before, and it's a great test of recognizing when a 'normal' data structure — a B-tree index on latitude/longitude columns — doesn't fit the access pattern, plus reasoning about a system where the data itself, everyone's location, is constantly moving.

functional: Riders can request a ride by specifying a pickup location and destination
System matches the rider with a nearby available driver
Both rider and driver see each other's live location during the trip
System estimates fare and ETA before and during the trip
nonFunctional: Millions of drivers reporting location every few seconds
Matching a rider to a driver should complete within a few seconds
Location data is high-volume and write-heavy, but only the latest position per driver matters much
Most queries are 'find things near this point' — a pattern a plain relational index handles poorly
Must stay available during regional demand spikes (e.g. a concert letting out) without falling over

hints: You need to answer 'which available drivers are within roughly 2km of this rider' very fast, many times a second, across millions of moving points. A plain lat/lng range query with a B-tree index doesn't do this efficiently. What kind of index structure is built for 2D proximity search?
Consider encoding a 2D lat/lng point into a single 1D string where nearby points tend to share a common prefix. That turns 'find nearby points' into a much cheaper prefix/range query.

Geohashing divides the map into a grid of cells, each with a short string code; a longer shared prefix means points are closer together, so you can query for all drivers whose geohash starts with the rider's cell prefix (and its neighbor cells, to catch points near a boundary). Store driver locations in an in-memory structure keyed by geohash for fast updates and lookups.
diagram:
flowchart TB
  Driver([Driver App]) -->|location every few sec| LocSvc[Location Service]
  LocSvc --> GeoIndex[(Geo Index\ngeohash -> driver_ids)]
  Rider([Rider App]) -->|request ride| MatchSvc[Matching Service]
  MatchSvc --> GeoIndex
  MatchSvc --> DriverDB[(Driver Status DB)]
  MatchSvc -->|offer| Driver
  MatchSvc --> TripSvc[Trip Service]
  TripSvc --> TripDB[(Trips DB)]
  TripSvc --> ETASvc[ETA / Pricing Service]

solution.approach:
**The core decision is the data structure for proximity search: geospatial indexing, because the natural query — 'which available drivers are within ~2km of this point' — doesn't fit a normal database index.** A standard B-tree index on latitude and longitude columns can accelerate a query on either column individually, but a 2D radius query needs both simultaneously, and a B-tree has no notion of 2D locality — rows with nearby lat/lng values aren't necessarily stored anywhere near each other in the index. You'd end up scanning a large swath of rows and filtering, which doesn't hold up at millions of moving points queried many times a second.

**Geohashing turns a 2D proximity problem into a 1D prefix-matching problem, which existing infrastructure handles well.** It works by recursively dividing the map into a grid, encoding each cell as a short base32 string (e.g. `9q8yy`); each additional character narrows the cell further, and two points that are geographically close usually share a long common prefix. 'Find drivers near this point' becomes 'find drivers whose geohash starts with this prefix,' a cheap range/prefix query rather than a full scan. The one wrinkle to handle explicitly: two points a few meters apart can fall on opposite sides of a cell boundary and get completely different prefixes, so a real query checks the rider's own cell plus its 8 neighboring cells to avoid missing a driver who's genuinely close but technically in an adjacent cell.

**The location update pipeline is extremely high-volume but each individual update has low lasting value, which should drive the storage choice.** Every driver's app pings a location service every few seconds; at millions of active drivers that's a huge sustained write rate, but for matching, only the latest position per driver matters — nobody queries 'where was this driver 10 minutes ago' for matching purposes. That points toward an in-memory, geo-indexed store (Redis with its native geospatial commands is a common real-world choice) for live positions, kept separate from a durable, disk-backed store written to less frequently for trip history and analytics, where the full location trail does matter.

**Matching is a fast, local, 'good enough' search, not a globally optimal assignment problem.** On a ride request, the matching service geo-queries nearby available drivers (starting at a tight radius and expanding it if too few candidates are found), ranks the handful of candidates by estimated distance or ETA, and sends a match offer to the top candidate with a short timeout — falling through to the next-ranked candidate if it's declined or times out. This deliberately isn't solving a global optimal-assignment problem across all riders and drivers in a region simultaneously; in a system where seconds matter, a fast, locally-good match beats a slower, theoretically-optimal one.

**The data model keeps live, volatile state separate from durable trip records.** `Drivers` (driver_id, status: available/en-route/offline, last-known geohash) captures current matchability. A separate hot store, keyed by geohash cell and holding the set of driver IDs currently in that cell, is what the matching query actually hits, updated on every location ping. `Trips` (trip_id, rider_id, driver_id, pickup, dropoff, status, fare) is the durable record of an actual ride, created once a match is confirmed, and lives in a normal relational store since it needs stronger consistency and doesn't churn nearly as fast as raw location data.

**ETA and pricing sit on top of the geospatial layer rather than being part of it.** At a high level, an ETA combines a route/distance estimate — potentially calling out to a dedicated routing/maps service using real road networks, not straight-line distance — with current traffic conditions; pricing typically factors in a base fare plus a supply/demand multiplier for the pickup area (surge pricing), which itself depends on knowing how many available drivers are nearby, directly fed by the same geo-index used for matching. These are meaningfully deep subsystems on their own, but the point here is recognizing that they consume the geospatial layer's output rather than needing to be designed from scratch.

**Regional partitioning is the main lever for scaling both the geo-index and the matching service.** A ride request in New York never needs to consider a driver in Los Angeles, so there's no reason for a single global geo-index or matching service instance to reason about the whole world at once. Sharding both by city or region bounds the working set each shard handles, lets regions scale independently, and keeps the geo-index for any one shard small enough to be efficiently served from memory.

**Consistency requirements differ sharply between the two kinds of state in this system.** Driver location is inherently a few seconds stale by the time it's queried — fine, positions don't need to be perfectly real-time for matching. Trip/driver-assignment state is the opposite: it needs strong consistency, because assigning the same driver to two overlapping trips is a real correctness bug — so confirming a match should be an atomic check-and-set on the driver's status (available -> assigned) rather than an eventually-consistent update.
keyPoints: Geohashing encodes 2D coordinates into a string where shared prefixes mean spatial proximity, turning 'find nearby' into a cheap prefix/range query
Check neighboring cells too, since two physically close points can fall on opposite sides of a geohash cell boundary
Live driver location is high-volume, low-durability-value data — keep it in an in-memory geo-indexed store, not the primary relational DB
Matching is a fast local search with a short offer timeout, not a global optimal assignment
Partition the geo-index and matching service by region/city — rides never match across city boundaries
Driver location can be eventually consistent; trip/driver-assignment state must be strongly consistent to avoid double-booking a driver

practicePrompt: A driver is right at a geohash cell boundary and a rider requests a pickup a block away, on the other side of that boundary. Walk through how your matching query still finds that driver, and what it costs you (extra cells queried, precision level) to handle this correctly.

title: Design a Video Streaming Service (YouTube)
statement:
Design the backend for a video platform like YouTube: users upload videos, the platform makes them available for streaming in a way that adapts to each viewer's network and device, and viewers around the world get a fast, low-buffering playback experience.

This question is asked because it covers a full pipeline — ingestion, asynchronous heavy processing, and global content delivery — and tests whether you'll reach for the right storage system for wildly different kinds of data (huge immutable video files vs. small, frequently-updated metadata) instead of forcing everything into one database.

functional: Users can upload a video file
The platform transcodes uploaded video into multiple resolutions/bitrates
Viewers can watch videos with playback quality that adapts to their network conditions
Users can search for and browse videos, seeing metadata like title, views, and likes
nonFunctional: Uploads of large files (GBs) need to be reliable and resumable
Millions of concurrent video streams globally, with low startup latency and minimal rebuffering
Storage is enormous (petabytes) and mostly write-once, read-many
Transcoding is CPU-intensive and can happen asynchronously — users tolerate a short delay before a video is watchable
Global audience — playback latency depends heavily on serving video close to the viewer

hints: A raw uploaded video file and its metadata (title, description, view count) have very different access patterns and sizes. Should they live in the same storage system?

Serving the same fixed-quality video to a viewer on fast fiber and one on a spotty mobile connection wastes bandwidth or causes rebuffering. What playback technique lets the client itself pick and switch quality levels mid-stream?

Store raw and transcoded video files as blobs in object storage, with metadata in a separate database. Transcode the upload into multiple resolutions/bitrates, each split into small chunks described by a manifest file (HLS/DASH); the client's player downloads chunks and switches quality between them based on measured bandwidth. Distribute chunks via a CDN so viewers stream from a nearby edge location, not origin storage.
diagram:
flowchart TB
  Uploader([Uploader]) -->|chunked upload| UploadSvc[Upload Service]
  UploadSvc --> RawStore[(Raw Video Blob Store)]
  UploadSvc --> Queue[Transcoding Queue]
  Queue --> Transcoder[Transcoding Workers]
  Transcoder --> EncodedStore[(Encoded Chunks\nmultiple bitrates)]
  Transcoder --> MetaDB[(Metadata DB\ntitle, status, views)]
  EncodedStore --> CDN[CDN Edge Cache]
  Viewer([Viewer]) -->|adaptive streaming| CDN
  Viewer --> MetaSvc[Metadata / Search Service]
  MetaSvc --> MetaDB

solution.approach:
**The core decision is splitting storage by access pattern: huge, immutable video files in blob storage, small, frequently-changing records in a metadata database.** A raw or transcoded video file is large (hundreds of MB to several GB), written once, and then read very many times without ever changing — a textbook fit for object storage like S3, built cheaply and durably for exactly this pattern. Metadata — title, description, transcoding status, view/like counts — is small, structured, frequently updated, and needs to support queries like 'videos by this creator, sorted by upload date' that a blob store can't answer efficiently. Forcing both into the same system fights the grain of both technologies.

**Upload needs to be chunked and resumable, because the files involved are large enough that a flaky connection failing partway through is the normal case, not an edge case.** The client splits the file into parts and uploads each independently with per-part retry, either reassembling them server-side or using the object store's native multipart upload support directly — either way, a dropped connection only costs the in-flight chunk, not the whole multi-gigabyte file. The upload request itself returns as soon as the raw file is safely stored and a transcoding job is enqueued — it does not block on transcoding, which can take much longer than a user would tolerate waiting on an HTTP response for.

**Transcoding is the CPU-intensive, asynchronous heart of the pipeline.** A pool of transcoding workers pulls jobs off a queue and converts the uploaded source into multiple resolution/bitrate variants (e.g. 1080p, 720p, 480p), splitting each variant into short segments (a few seconds each) rather than one long file per resolution. This work is embarrassingly parallel — different videos transcode completely independently, and even segments of the same video can be transcoded in parallel — so the worker pool scales horizontally with queue depth. On completion, a manifest file (HLS's `.m3u8` or DASH's `.mpd`) is written, listing the available quality variants and the URLs for their segments, and the video's metadata status flips to 'ready.'

**Adaptive bitrate streaming is a client-driven mechanic that the segmenting above exists to support.** The player downloads the manifest first, starts playback at a conservative quality level, and continuously measures the actual throughput it's achieving while downloading segments — if bandwidth is healthy, it requests the next segment at a higher quality; if it's degrading, it drops down. Because each segment is short and self-contained, a quality switch only costs the next segment's worth of latency rather than requiring a full re-buffer or restart — this is the entire reason video is transcoded into short chunks instead of one file per resolution.

**A CDN is what makes global low-latency playback possible, and video is about as cache-friendly a workload as exists.** Transcoded segments are immutable once created and, for any reasonably popular video, read enormously more often than they're written — an ideal fit for edge caching. Segments are distributed to CDN edge locations, so a viewer streams from a nearby edge node rather than round-tripping to origin storage on every request. This also protects origin storage from load, since only genuine cache misses ever reach it.

**The data model reflects the split from the first point.** `Videos` (video_id, uploader_id, title, description, status, duration, created_at) plus a manifest referencing segment URLs make up the metadata side; view counts and other high-frequency engagement metrics are usually not updated with a strict row increment per view — at meaningful scale that's an enormous write rate for a number nobody needs to the exact unit in real time — instead they're aggregated asynchronously and periodically flushed to the durable count.

**The two main scaling axes are transcoding compute and storage cost, and they call for different techniques.** Transcoding worker capacity scales elastically with queue depth, and can be prioritized if capacity is ever constrained during a burst of uploads. Storage cost, at petabyte scale, benefits from tiering — videos that go months without a view can move to cheaper, higher-latency cold storage, accepting a slower time-to-first-byte on rare access, while actively-watched content stays on hot storage and in the CDN.
keyPoints: Split storage: huge immutable video blobs in object storage, small mutable structured records in a metadata database
Uploads are chunked and resumable so a large file doesn't need to restart from scratch on a network blip
Transcoding runs asynchronously after upload, converting the source into multiple resolutions/bitrates split into short chunks
Adaptive bitrate streaming lets the client switch quality between chunks based on measured bandwidth, guided by a manifest (HLS/DASH)
A CDN caches chunks at edge locations near viewers, since video is read-heavy, immutable, and highly cacheable
View counts and engagement metrics are extremely high-write-volume and usually aggregated asynchronously rather than updated per view

practicePrompt: A video goes viral within an hour of upload, while it's still being transcoded into lower-resolution variants. Should viewers be blocked from watching until all resolutions are ready, or is there a way to let them start watching sooner? Sketch how you'd handle that.

title: Design a Web Crawler
statement:
Design a web crawler that starts from a set of seed URLs, downloads pages, extracts the links on each page, and continues crawling outward — eventually covering a substantial fraction of the public web — without hammering any single website into the ground or crawling the same page over and over.

This question is asked because it's a good vehicle for reasoning about a work queue that needs both priority and fairness constraints at once (politeness per domain), and for recognizing when an exact data structure — a hash set of every URL ever seen — is the wrong tool at extreme scale, in favor of a probabilistic one.

functional: Given a set of seed URLs, discover and download web pages by following links
Extract new URLs from downloaded pages and queue them for crawling
Avoid re-crawling the same URL repeatedly, or re-crawl on a sane schedule
Respect each site's crawling rules (robots.txt) and avoid overwhelming any one domain
nonFunctional: Crawl billions of pages
Be a 'polite' crawler — bounded requests/sec to any single domain, so as not to be mistaken for a DDoS or get IP-banned
Fault tolerant — a crawl running over days/weeks must survive individual worker crashes without losing progress
Efficient dedup at massive scale — checking 'have I seen this URL' must not become the bottleneck
Extensible to prioritize important or fresh pages over low-value ones

hints: The frontier of URLs to crawl next isn't just a plain FIFO queue — if it were, a domain with millions of pages would monopolize your crawler's attention and hammer that one server. What structure lets you both prioritize and rate-limit per domain?

Checking 'have I already crawled this exact URL' against billions of seen URLs, on every discovered link, needs to be fast and memory-cheap. An exact set stored in a normal database won't keep up. What probabilistic data structure trades a small false-positive rate for huge space savings?

Use a front queue (priority by crawl importance) feeding into a back queue system with one queue per host, and a scheduler that only pulls from a host's queue if enough time has passed since its last request. For dedup, use a Bloom filter to cheaply reject URLs that have almost certainly already been seen, backed by an exact store for the rare cases you need to double check.
diagram:
flowchart TB
  Seeds([Seed URLs]) --> Frontier[URL Frontier\npriority + per-host queues]
  Frontier --> Scheduler[Politeness Scheduler]
  Scheduler --> Worker1[Crawl Worker]
  Scheduler --> Worker2[Crawl Worker]
  Worker1 --> Fetch[Fetcher\nrespects robots.txt]
  Fetch --> PageStore[(Page Store)]
  Fetch --> Extractor[Link Extractor]
  Extractor --> BloomFilter[(Bloom Filter\nseen URLs)]
  BloomFilter -.new.-> Frontier
  Extractor --> URLDB[(Exact URL Store)]

solution.approach:
**The core decision is the URL frontier's structure, which has to satisfy two competing needs at once: prioritizing important pages, and never overwhelming any one website.** A plain FIFO queue fails immediately: if a single domain happens to have millions of discoverable pages, it would dominate the queue and get crawled continuously while every other domain starves, and hitting one site with a continuous stream of requests looks like an attack. The standard structure is two-tiered: front queues, which hold URLs bucketed/ordered by priority (a rough score of how important or fresh a page is likely to be), feeding into back queues, where there's exactly one queue per host, guaranteeing all pending URLs for a given site are grouped together and giving a natural place to throttle that specific host.

**Politeness is enforced at the back-queue layer, explicitly, not as an afterthought.** A scheduler tracks, per host, the last time a request was sent to it, and only pulls a URL from that host's back queue once a minimum interval has passed — a URL sitting in a 'not yet ready' host queue simply waits, without blocking crawl workers from making progress on other, ready hosts. Before fetching anything from a host, the crawler also fetches and caches that host's `robots.txt` and filters out disallowed paths, both as a matter of correctness and to avoid crawling content the site owner explicitly excluded.

**Deduplication at this scale needs a probabilistic structure, because an exact one doesn't fit in a reasonable amount of memory.** Every link extracted from every crawled page needs a fast 'have I already queued or crawled this URL' check, and at billions of URLs, an exact structure — a hash set backed by a database — is both memory-expensive and slower per lookup than this hot path can tolerate. A Bloom filter — a fixed-size bit array plus several hash functions — answers 'definitely not seen' or 'maybe already seen' in constant time with a small, tunable false-positive rate, using a small fraction of the memory an exact set would need. The trade-off — occasionally, rarely, skipping a URL that wasn't actually seen before — is acceptable for a crawler covering a huge corpus, and it's backed by an exact URL store for cases that need certainty or for periodically rebuilding the filter.

**The crawl loop itself is straightforward once the frontier and dedup pieces exist.** A worker pulls a URL from whichever host queue is currently ready, fetches the page (handling timeouts, redirects, and transient failures with retry/backoff), stores the raw content, and runs a link extractor over it.
