Extracted links are normalized — resolving relative URLs against the page's base URL, stripping fragments and tracking query parameters that don't actually change the resource — before being checked against the Bloom filter; genuinely new URLs get pushed back into the frontier, closing the loop.

**Durability matters because a real crawl runs for days or weeks, not minutes, and has to survive individual worker crashes without losing progress.** The frontier's queue state and the seen-URL store both need to live in durable storage — a persistent queue system, a real database or distributed KV store for the Bloom filter's backing structure and the exact-URL fallback — rather than purely in a worker's memory. A lease/checkpoint mechanism, where a URL claimed by a worker is marked 'in progress' with a timeout, ensures a crashed worker's in-flight URL gets released and requeued rather than lost entirely.

**Distributing the crawl across many nodes is done by partitioning on host, which keeps politeness enforcement simple.** Hashing the host portion of a URL to decide which crawler node owns that host's back queue and rate-limiting state means all requests to a given domain are coordinated by a single node — no need for cross-node locking just to enforce 'don't hit this host too fast,' since the enforcement never has to span nodes for any single host.

**Priority is a pluggable scoring function layered on top of the mechanism above, not baked into it.** A page's priority score for the front queues can incorporate signals like inbound link count, how frequently a page's content tends to change, or business-specific signals — but none of that changes how the back queues, politeness scheduler, or dedup filter work; it only changes which URL gets pulled first when multiple are ready.
keyPoints: The URL frontier is two-tiered: front queues for priority, back queues (one per host) for per-domain ordering and politeness
Politeness means respecting robots.txt and rate-limiting requests per host so the crawler isn't mistaken for an attack or IP-banned
A Bloom filter gives cheap, memory-efficient 'probably already seen' checks at billions-of-URLs scale, accepting rare false positives
Partition the frontier and dedup state by host hash so politeness enforcement for a given domain stays on one node
Frontier and seen-URL state must be durable, not purely in-memory, so a multi-day crawl survives worker restarts
Crawl priority is a pluggable scoring function layered on top of the core frontier mechanism, separate from politeness/dedup

practicePrompt: Your crawler discovers 10,000 new URLs from a single page, all on the same domain that already has a slow, rate-limited back queue. Walk through what happens to those URLs — where do they sit, and how does your design prevent them from starving URLs discovered on other, less-crawled domains?

title: Design a Parking Lot System
statement:
Design the software for a multi-level parking garage: it needs to track which spots are free, assign an appropriately-sized spot to an arriving vehicle (motorcycles, cars, and buses all need different spot sizes), issue a ticket, and compute the fee when the vehicle leaves.

Unlike most of the other questions in this set, this one is intentionally **not** about distributed systems or scale — it's an object-oriented design (OOD) question, asked because it tests a different, equally important skill: can you take a real-world problem and decompose it into a small set of well-encapsulated classes with clear responsibilities, so that new vehicle types or pricing rules can be added later without rewriting the core logic.

functional: Support multiple vehicle types (motorcycle, car, bus) that require different spot sizes
Assign an available, appropriately-sized spot to an entering vehicle and issue a ticket
Compute the fee owed when a vehicle exits, based on duration and vehicle type
Track real-time availability of spots by level and by size
Support multiple entry/exit points and multiple levels
nonFunctional: Spot assignment must be correct — never assign the same spot to two vehicles at once
Easy to extend with new pricing schemes (flat rate vs hourly, weekday vs weekend) without rewriting core logic
Easy to add new vehicle types or spot types later
Entry/exit operations should be fast even with thousands of spots — no full-lot scan

hints: This one's about class design, not infrastructure. Start with the nouns in the problem: what real-world things need to become classes, and what behavior belongs on which one?

A motorcycle can technically fit in a compact or a large spot, but a bus can't fit in a compact one. Model spot sizes and vehicle sizes as a shared, ordered concept with a compatibility rule, rather than hardcoding if/else checks for every vehicle type in your assignment logic.

Core classes: Vehicle (with a Size), ParkingSpot (with a Size and occupied state), Ticket (links a Vehicle to a Spot with entry time), Level (holds spots, tracks free-spot counts per size for fast lookup), ParkingLot (holds levels, orchestrates entry/exit). Make pricing a separate strategy object that the exit flow calls, so new pricing schemes plug in without touching spot-assignment logic.
diagram:
flowchart TB
  Vehicle([Vehicle\nmotorcycle, car, bus]) -->|enters| EntryPanel[Entry Panel]
  EntryPanel --> Lot[ParkingLot]
  Lot --> Level1[Level]
  Level1 --> SpotMgr[Spot Manager\nfree counts by size]
  SpotMgr -->|assign| Spot[ParkingSpot]
  EntryPanel --> Ticket[Ticket\nvehicle, spot, entry_time]
  Vehicle -->|exits| ExitPanel[Exit Panel]
  ExitPanel --> Ticket
  ExitPanel --> Pricing[Pricing Strategy]
  Pricing -->|fee| Payment[Payment]
  ExitPanel --> SpotMgr

solution.approach:
**Unlike the rest of this set, the hard part here isn't throughput or failure tolerance — it's picking the right nouns and giving each one a single, clear responsibility.** Reading the problem statement, the classes fall out fairly directly: a Vehicle (of some size), a ParkingSpot (of some size, with occupied/free state), a Ticket (linking a vehicle to a spot with an entry timestamp), a Level (a collection of spots, plus some way to find a free one quickly), a ParkingLot (a collection of levels, the top-level entry point for entry/exit flows), and a pricing component deliberately kept separate from all of the above.

**The one real design insight is modeling vehicle and spot sizes as a shared, ordered concept rather than special-casing every vehicle type.** Define a Size (say, Motorcycle < Compact < Large) that both Vehicle and ParkingSpot carry, and a single compatibility rule — a vehicle can park in any spot whose size is greater than or equal to its own — instead of writing separate conditional logic for 'if it's a bus, look for a large spot; if it's a car, look for a compact or large spot...' scattered through the assignment code. Every new vehicle type added later just needs a Size, and the existing assignment logic handles it correctly with zero changes — this is the difference between a design that scales cleanly with new requirements and one that accumulates special cases.

**Fast spot assignment comes from maintaining an index, not from scanning.** Rather than searching through every spot on the level looking for a free one of the right size — which would get slow with thousands of spots — each Level maintains a free-spot index: a map from Size to a set or queue of currently-free spot IDs of that size. Assigning a spot becomes an O(1) pop from the right size's free list, falling back to the next larger size's list if the exact size is full, and releasing a spot on exit is an O(1) push back onto its list — this is the data-structure-level answer to the 'no full-lot scan' requirement.

**The entry flow is where the one genuine concurrency hazard in this otherwise sequential design shows up.** A vehicle arrives, the entry panel determines its size, asks the ParkingLot/Level to find and reserve a spot of at least that size, creates a Ticket (vehicle, spot, entry timestamp), and marks the spot occupied. If two vehicles arrive at the same instant, the 'find and reserve' step has to be atomic — the pop from the free-spot index needs to be a single atomic operation so two vehicles can never be handed the same spot ID; everything else in this design can be reasoned about as purely sequential, but this one step can't be.

**Exit and pricing is where the design's extensibility requirement gets satisfied directly.** On exit, the Ticket is looked up and the duration is computed from its entry timestamp — but the actual fee calculation is delegated to a PricingStrategy object rather than being hardcoded into the exit handler. Defining PricingStrategy as an interface with a single calculateFee(ticket) method means concrete implementations — HourlyPricingStrategy, FlatRatePricingStrategy, a decorator that adds a weekend surcharge — can be swapped in, composed, or added later without touching the entry/exit orchestration code at all. This is the textbook case for the Strategy pattern: an algorithm expected to vary should be pulled out from the code that uses it.

**Multi-level and multi-entry-point support falls out naturally once state lives in the right place.** ParkingLot aggregates multiple Level objects, each independently maintaining its own free-spot index so lookups stay fast and localized rather than needing a single lot-wide structure. Multiple physical entry/exit panels are just separate, stateless callers into the same shared ParkingLot API — the actual state (which spots are free) has exactly one source of truth, so it doesn't matter how many physical kiosks are calling into it concurrently, as long as the reservation step stays atomic.

**New spot types are handled as attributes, not a parallel class hierarchy.** Something like an EV-charging spot or a handicap-accessible spot isn't really a new size — it's an additional tag/attribute on ParkingSpot that assignment logic can filter or prefer on, alongside the size-based compatibility rule, rather than requiring a whole new spot subclass with its own matching logic. Keeping size (which drives the core fit/no-fit rule) and other attributes (which drive preference/eligibility) as separate concerns keeps the assignment logic from growing a combinatorial explosion of spot-type-specific branches.

**It's worth explicitly contrasting this with the rest of the question set: there's no sharding, no replication, no distributed consensus here**, unless the exercise were extended to a multi-building fleet with shared state across locations. The entire difficulty is choosing abstractions — a shared size hierarchy, an indexed free-spot lookup, a pluggable pricing strategy — that keep assignment, pricing, and multi-level support each able to change independently without rippling into the others.
keyPoints: Model vehicle and spot sizes with a shared, ordered Size concept and one compatibility rule, instead of type-specific if/else logic
Maintain a free-spot index per size (not a full scan) so assignment and release are O(1) operations
Pull fee calculation out into a PricingStrategy interface so new pricing schemes plug in without touching entry/exit flow
A Ticket is the join record between Vehicle, ParkingSpot, and time — the exit flow looks it up to compute duration and fee
Spot assignment must be atomic at the point of reservation — the one real concurrency hazard in an otherwise sequential design
Multiple levels and entry/exit panels are stateless callers into one shared ParkingLot state, so spot data has a single source of truth
This question tests object-oriented decomposition and encapsulation, not throughput or distributed coordination

practicePrompt: A motorcycle pulls in and every motorcycle-sized spot is full, but compact and large spots are open. Should your assignment logic let it take a compact spot? Sketch the compatibility rule between Size levels that answers this, and think about whether you'd ever want to reserve larger spots for larger vehicles by *not* always falling back automatically.

title: Design a Key-Value Store (like DynamoDB)

tradeoffs.question: Under a network partition, what gives?

options.name: CP (Consistency over Availability)
options.pros: Every read reflects the latest acknowledged write - no conflicting versions to resolve
options.cons: Some nodes must reject requests during a partition, hurting availability

options.name: AP (Availability over Consistency)
options.pros: Keeps accepting reads and writes through a partition
options.cons: Concurrent writes during the partition can produce conflicting versions of a key that must be resolved later

statement:
Design a distributed key-value store — a simplified version of Amazon DynamoDB — that stores arbitrary key-value pairs across a cluster of commodity machines, stays available and accepts writes even during network partitions or node failures, and lets clients tune the consistency/latency trade-off per request.

This question is asked because it's the deepest dive in this set into the CAP theorem in practice: rather than discussing consistency vs. availability abstractly, you have to design the actual mechanism — quorums, versioning, conflict resolution — that makes 'available, eventually consistent, occasionally conflicting' a concrete, implementable system rather than a buzzword.

functional: Simple put(key, value) and get(key) operations exposed to clients
Data is automatically partitioned across many nodes as the dataset grows
Data is replicated across nodes so it survives node/rack/datacenter failures
Tunable consistency — clients can choose stronger or weaker consistency/latency trade-offs per request
nonFunctional: Massive scale — petabytes of data, millions of ops/sec
High availability — favor availability over strict consistency (an AP system in CAP terms), accepting writes even during partial failures
Low, predictable latency — single-digit milliseconds for both reads and writes
No single point of failure — fully decentralized, no special master node whose failure takes down the cluster
Must handle concurrent writes to the same key from different clients/replicas gracefully

hints: With replication, more than one node can accept a write for the same key, possibly while another replica is unreachable. What lets you make writes/reads tunably reliable without requiring every single replica to be up and in agreement every time?

Think in terms of three numbers: how many replicas you write to before acknowledging a write, how many you read from before returning a value, and how many total replicas exist. What relationship between them guarantees a read sees the latest write?

Quorum replication: with N replicas per key, a write succeeds after W replicas ack it, and a read queries R replicas and returns the most recent. Setting W + R > N guarantees any read overlaps with the latest write's replica set. Because replicas can still diverge under concurrent writes or partitions, use vector clocks (or simpler last-write-wins with timestamps) to detect and resolve conflicting versions of a key. Partition keys with consistent hashing, but now each partition is replicated to N nodes around the ring.
diagram:
flowchart TB
  Client([Client]) --> Coordinator[Coordinator Node]
  Coordinator --> Ring[Consistent Hash Ring]
  Ring --> NodeA[Node A]
  Ring --> NodeB[Node B]
  Ring --> NodeC[Node C]
  Coordinator -->|write, wait for W acks| NodeA
  Coordinator -->|write, wait for W acks| NodeB
  Coordinator -->|write, wait for W acks| NodeC
  Coordinator -->|read from R replicas| NodeA
  NodeA --> VersionStore[(Versioned Store\nvector clocks)]
  Coordinator --> Gossip[Gossip Protocol\nmembership and failure detection]

solution.approach:
**The core decision is quorum-based replication, because it's what lets the system keep accepting writes during partial failures — the defining requirement of an AP system.** With N replicas held for every key, a write is acknowledged to the client once W of those replicas have confirmed it (not all N), and a read queries R replicas and returns the most recent value among their responses. W and R are tunable per request or per table: a workload that wants fast, highly available writes and can tolerate slightly stale reads might use W=1, R=N; one that wants guaranteed-fresh reads might use W=N, R=1; a balanced default like N=3, W=2, R=2 is common. The key guarantee is that whenever W + R > N, any read's set of R replicas is mathematically guaranteed to overlap with any write's set of W replicas by at least one node — so a read is guaranteed to see the most recently acknowledged write, even though it never talked to all N replicas.

**Partitioning uses the same consistent hashing as a distributed cache, extended with a preference list.** Keys and nodes are hashed onto a ring, with virtual nodes for even distribution — but instead of one owning node per key, each position on the ring maps to a preference list of N distinct nodes (the primary owner, plus the next N-1 nodes walking clockwise), which together hold all replicas of that key's data. Adding or removing a node still only reassigns a bounded slice of the ring, exactly as in the single-copy cache case, just now affecting a slice of preference lists rather than single ownership assignments.

**On the write path, any node can act as coordinator — there's no special master whose failure takes anything down.** A client's write for a key can be handled by whichever node it happens to contact; that node determines the key's preference list, forwards the write to all N replicas in parallel, and returns success to the client as soon as W of them acknowledge — it doesn't wait for the remaining replicas, which continue being updated asynchronously in the background. This is what keeps write latency low and availability high even when one replica is temporarily slow or unreachable: the client never waits on the slowest node in the list, only the W-th fastest.

**The read path is symmetric, and it's where conflicting versions of a key actually surface.** A coordinator queries R replicas for the key and compares what comes back. If all R responses agree, that's simply the answer. If they disagree — which can genuinely happen, since different write requests may have reached different subsets of replicas, especially around a network partition — the coordinator has to reconcile multiple versions of the same key before it can respond, which is exactly the conflict-resolution problem below.

**Conflict resolution is necessary specifically because this system chose availability over strict consistency.** The simplest approach is last-write-wins, using a timestamp attached to every write and keeping whichever is newest — easy to implement, but it can silently discard a legitimate concurrent update if two writes' timestamps are close or clocks are imperfectly synced. Vector clocks are the more rigorous tool: each replica tracks a per-node version counter for the key, which lets the system distinguish a write that's a clear causal descendant of another (safe to resolve automatically, keep the newer one) from two writes that are genuinely concurrent — neither happened-before the other, meaning they represent an actual conflict that needs real reconciliation, either an app-specific merge (like combining two versions of a shopping cart's item list) or surfacing both versions to the client/application to decide.

**Node failures are handled at two different timescales.** For transient failures — a replica briefly unreachable during a write — hinted handoff keeps W achievable: the coordinator writes to a different, healthy node instead, tagging the write with a hint that it actually belongs to the down replica; once that replica recovers, the hinted write is replayed to it, and the temporary stand-in can drop its copy. For longer-term drift — a replica that missed a batch of updates while it was down — an anti-entropy process periodically compares replicas, efficiently, using Merkle trees to diff hash trees of the data rather than comparing every key individually, and repairs whichever replica is behind.

**Decentralized membership via gossip is what avoids reintroducing a single point of failure at the coordination layer.** Rather than a central registry of which nodes are up and where they sit on the ring, nodes periodically exchange state with a few random peers, and this peer-to-peer information exchange converges the whole cluster's view of membership and health over time without any node being special or required. This is consistent with the 'any node can coordinate any request' property from the write/read paths above — there's no leader anywhere in this design.

**The trade-off, stated plainly, is complexity and occasional conflicts in exchange for availability and tunable latency.** A single-leader, strongly consistent system — a traditional relational database — is simpler to reason about, since a client always reads the latest acknowledged write, but the leader is a bottleneck and a single point of unavailability during a failure or partition. This quorum-based design accepts more moving parts (versioning, conflict resolution, hinted handoff, anti-entropy) in exchange for staying available and responsive through exactly the failure conditions that would stall a single-leader system — the right choice for workloads like session stores, shopping carts, and sensor/event data that can tolerate and meaningfully resolve an occasional conflicting read, though not for workloads that fundamentally require every reader to see a single, immediately-consistent truth.
keyPoints: Quorum replication (N replicas, W acks on write, R reads) with W + R > N guarantees a read overlaps with the latest acknowledged write, without needing all N replicas available
The system trades strict consistency for availability (AP) — it keeps accepting writes during partial failures, which is what makes conflicting versions of a key possible
Consistent hashing partitions keys across nodes; each ring position maps to a preference list of N nodes, not just one
Vector clocks (or simpler last-write-wins) detect and resolve divergent versions of a key caused by concurrent or partition-era writes
Hinted handoff keeps writes succeeding through transient node failures; anti-entropy via Merkle trees repairs replicas afterward
No special master node — any node can coordinate a request, and gossip protocols keep membership/failure state decentralized
N/W/R are tunable per request or per table, letting different workloads trade off latency, consistency, and availability differently

practicePrompt: With N=3, W=2, R=2, walk through what happens to a get(key) request if two different coordinators each accepted a concurrent put(key, value) against different, overlapping-but-not-identical pairs of replicas during a brief network hiccup. What does the read return, and how does your conflict-resolution mechanism decide?
